title: Networking II: Wireshark and packet capture
description: Capture, filter and analyze network traffic with Wireshark and tcpdump.

1.title: Capturing and filtering: Wireshark basics
1.body:
## Your first capture

1. Open Wireshark → select your active interface (eth0/wlan0)
2. Click Start (blue icon)
3. Browse to any website → you'll see packets in real time
4. Stop (red icon)

## Display Filters (your everyday tool)

```text
http                          → HTTP only
tcp.port == 443               → HTTPS only
ip.addr == 10.10.10.5         → traffic to/from that IP
ip.src == 10.10.10.5          → only traffic from that IP
dns                           → DNS queries only
tcp.flags.syn == 1            → SYNs only (connection starts)
http.request.method == "POST" → POSTs only
!(http or dns)                → everything EXCEPT HTTP and DNS
```

## The 3-pane layout

```text
┌──────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ 1. Packet List: one packet per line      │
│    (no., time, source, dest, protocol)   │
├──────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ 2. Packet Details: the protocol layers   │
│    (Ethernet → IP → TCP → HTTP → Data)   │
│    Click ▶ to expand each layer          │
├──────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ 3. Packet Bytes: the raw hex dump        │
│    (what literally travels)              │
└──────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

**Right-click a packet → Follow → TCP Stream**: rebuilds the complete conversation
in plain text. It's the fastest way to see HTTP credentials, FTP commands
or Telnet sessions.

redes-wireshark-t01-q01.prompt: Which Wireshark filter shows ONLY HTTP traffic?
redes-wireshark-t01-q01.hint: The protocol name in the display filter.

redes-wireshark-t01-q02.prompt: Which display filter shows only the traffic to/from the IP 10.10.10.5?

redes-wireshark-t01-q03.prompt: What is 'promiscuous mode' in network capture?
redes-wireshark-t01-q03.hint: Listening to ALL the traffic on the network, not just what's addressed to you.

options.b: The interface captures ALL packets passing through it, not just those addressed to your MAC

2.title: Analysis: finding credentials in traffic
2.body:
## Finding gold in the capture

### HTTP Basic Auth
```text
Filter: http.authorization
Click the packet → HTTP → Authorization: Basic dXNlcjpwYXNzd29yZA==
Base64 decode: user:password
```

### FTP (credentials in cleartext)
```text
Filter: ftp
You'll see: USER anonymous
            PASS user@example.com
            USER admin
            PASS SuperSecret123  ← in plain text!
```

### Telnet (everything in cleartext)
```text
Filter: telnet
Follow TCP Stream → the full session as text: login, password, commands
```

## TCP Stream: the reconstruction

**Right-click any TCP packet → Follow → TCP Stream**:

```text
POST /login HTTP/1.1
Host: app.victima.com
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded

username=admin&password=P@ssw0rd123   ← the password in cleartext
```

It's the #1 tool of the traffic analyst — and of the attacker on the same network (MITM).

## TLS/HTTPS: what you CAN'T see

```text
Transport Layer Security    (port 443)
├── Client Hello            (visible: SNI = domain)
├── Server Hello + Cert     (visible: certificate)
├── Key Exchange            (visible: public parameters)
└── Encrypted Data          (INVISIBLE without the key)
```

With TLS, Wireshark only shows metadata (IPs, the domain via SNI, sizes). The
content stays encrypted — that's why HTTPS is essential. To see TLS content
you need the server's private key (or a TLS proxy such as Burp/mitmproxy).

## tcpdump: Wireshark without a GUI

```bash
# Capture on a specific interface
tcpdump -i eth0 -w captura.pcap          # save to a file (open it in Wireshark)
tcpdump -i eth0 port 80                  # HTTP only
tcpdump -i eth0 host 10.10.10.5          # a single IP only
tcpdump -i eth0 -A port 21               # FTP in ASCII (credentials!)
```

On servers without a GUI, tcpdump captures → you download the .pcap → you open it in
Wireshark on your own machine.

redes-wireshark-t02-q01.prompt: Which protocol sends credentials IN PLAIN TEXT over the network?
redes-wireshark-t02-q01.hint: HTTP Basic Auth, FTP, Telnet — no encryption.

options.b: HTTP Basic Auth, FTP, Telnet — all unencrypted

redes-wireshark-t02-q02.prompt: Which Wireshark option rebuilds a complete TCP conversation?

redes-wireshark-t02-q03.prompt: Why doesn't Wireshark show the content of an HTTPS connection if you don't have the server's key?
redes-wireshark-t02-q03.hint: Look at the tree in "TLS/HTTPS: what you CAN'T see": which parts stay visible and which one doesn't?

options.a: Because Wireshark can't capture traffic on port 443
options.b: Because HTTPS compresses packets and Wireshark can't decompress them
options.c: Because TLS encrypts the application layer: without the key the content can't be decrypted
options.d: Because promiscuous mode drops encrypted packets

3.title: Lab: hunting credentials in captures
3.body:
## Three captures, three sins

The lab serves real `.pcap` captures (generated packet by packet). Download them and
open them in Wireshark — or analyze them with `strings`/`grep` if you don't have a GUI:

```bash
curl -O http://127.0.0.1:18104/capture-http.pcap
curl -O http://127.0.0.1:18104/capture-ftp.pcap
curl -O http://127.0.0.1:18104/capture-dns.pcap
```

## Sin 1: plain HTTP with Basic Auth

Basic Auth sends `base64(usuario:contraseña)` — and base64 **is not encryption**,
it's encoding. Over HTTP (without TLS) the credentials travel in cleartext on every
request:

```bash
# In Wireshark: filter  http.authorization
# Without Wireshark:
grep -a "Basic" capture-http.pcap | grep -o "Basic [A-Za-z0-9+/=]*"
echo "YWRtaW46..." | base64 -d      # → admin:FLAG{...}
```

**Lesson**: without HTTPS, Basic Auth means shouting your password.

## Sin 2: FTP

FTP authenticates in cleartext by design (1990): the `USER` and `PASS` commands
travel in readable form. Filter `ftp.pass` in Wireshark and you'll see the password
right there in the dissection pane.

```bash
grep -ao "PASS [A-Za-z0-9{}_.-]*" capture-ftp.pcap
```

**Lesson**: FTP is still alive on internal networks; SFTP/FTPS exist for a reason.

## Sin 3: DNS tunnel

HTTP traffic to strange IPs gets blocked... but DNS always gets through. In the
capture, several queries to `tunnel.evil-c2.example` carry **base32-encoded
subdomains** with exfiltrated data:

```bash
# In Wireshark: filter  dns && dns.qry.name contains "tunnel"
# The long subdomains, concatenated (without session-start./data/.chunk2), are base32:
echo "<subdominio-completo>" | base32 -d
```

Base32 (A-Z, 2-7) was chosen here precisely because those characters are valid
in DNS labels. **Lesson**: monitor DNS queries with abnormally long,
high-entropy labels.

redes-wireshark-t03-q01.prompt: Download capture-http.pcap from the lab and find the credentials in the Authorization: Basic header. What is the password travelling in base64?
redes-wireshark-t03-q01.hint: curl -O http://127.0.0.1:18104/capture-http.pcap — search for 'Basic' and decode it: echo <b64> | base64 -d

redes-wireshark-t03-q02.prompt: In capture-ftp.pcap, which password does the user backup_svc send in cleartext?
redes-wireshark-t03-q02.hint: FTP encrypts NOTHING: filter ftp.pass in Wireshark or search for 'PASS' with strings/grep

redes-wireshark-t03-q03.prompt: capture-dns.pcap contains a DNS tunnel to tunnel.evil-c2.example. Concatenate the long subdomains (removing session-start./data) and decode the base32. Submit the flag.
redes-wireshark-t03-q03.hint: echo <concatenated-subdomain> | base32 -d — the parts are split between the session-start.* query and the *.data.* query
